1324.title: The Kalachakra
1324.hook: the wheel of time teaching, given to huge crowds as a blessing for peace
1324.howItsDone: The Kalachakra initiation is given by senior lamas, including the Dalai Lama, often to very large gatherings; monks build a sand mandala for it, and some attend as a blessing and an offering for world peace rather than to take up the full practice.

segments.voice: Last week ended beside a deathbed, with a book read aloud. Your line: read aloud. A new week starts now.

A field at the edge of a town is filling up. Monks and nuns in maroon. Farmers who walked in from the hills. Families with thermoses and blankets, visitors from far away sitting cross-legged in the dust. In a hall nearby, a few monks lean over a low table, tapping colored sand from thin metal funnels, grain by grain, into a huge circular pattern. When the teaching begins, the crowd stretches so far back that from the last rows the stage is a speck. Some in that crowd won't follow every word. They came anyway. This is a Kalachakra.
screen: `A FIELD FILLING WITH PEOPLE.` → `SAND TAPPED GRAIN BY GRAIN.` → `THEY CAME ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Kalachakra is Sanskrit: kala, time, and chakra, wheel. The wheel of time. It names a tantra, a long and demanding Vajrayana teaching, and the awakened figure at its center. Tradition says the Buddha taught it, and that it was kept for generations in a hidden kingdom called Shambhala before it came to India and then to Tibet. The teaching speaks of time on more than one level. Outer time: the sky, the planets, the turning year; Tibetan calendars have leaned on its reckoning. Inner time: the body, its breath and its rhythms. And a third, called the other Kalachakra: the practice that sees through both and wakes up inside them. One wheel, seen from the stars, from the body, and from the mind. Then the crowds. Tantric initiations are traditionally given to committed students, but senior lamas, the Dalai Lama among them, have given the Kalachakra to very large gatherings. Some who come don't intend to take up the full practice. Teachers describe their being there as receiving a blessing, a seed planted, and the gathering itself as an offering for peace in the world. And the sand. The mandala the monks build with such care is swept up when the teaching ends, and the colored sand is often poured into running water, carrying the blessing outward. The wheel of time, made visible, and then let go.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where there is fighting or fear right now, a country in the news, a street, a home you know, and hold it gently, the way you'd hold a cup that's too full. If you pray, offer a prayer for peace from your own tradition, in words you already know; if you don't, simply hold the wish that this place could know peace, and breathe with it.
The Kalachakra. The wheel of time: a Vajrayana teaching on outer, inner and awakened time, given to great crowds as a blessing for peace. Today's word.
Your line: the wheel of time. Even swept-up sand travels on. Rest well.

1325.title: Tulkus
1325.hook: teachers recognized as rebirths of earlier masters
1325.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, when certain teachers die, senior lamas search for their rebirth using letters, dreams, signs and tests with the teacher's belongings; a recognized child, called a tulku, is then raised and educated in the monastery.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kalachakra, the wheel of time, and a sand mandala swept away. Your line: the wheel of time.

A few visitors arrive at a farmhouse, dressed plainly. On a table they set down some objects in pairs: two rosaries, two walking sticks, two small drums. One of each pair belonged to a teacher who died some years before; the other is a look-alike. A small child toddles over, studies them, and reaches, without much fuss, for the ones that were the teacher's. The visitors glance at each other. Scenes like this are told in the stories of how a tulku is found. It isn't the whole process, and it isn't proof on its own. But it is how a search can end.
screen: `OBJECTS SET IN PAIRS.` → `A CHILD REACHES FOR THE TEACHER'S.` → `THE SEARCH ENDS.`

segments.voice: Tulku is the Tibetan word used to translate the Sanskrit nirmanakaya, the emanation body: the form in which awakened mind appears in the world. In everyday Tibetan use, a tulku is a teacher recognized as the rebirth of an earlier master. In Buddhist teaching, beings are ordinarily carried into rebirth by their karma. A tulku is understood differently: a teacher who, out of compassion, chooses to return, to carry on the work with the same students and the same monastery. The Dalai Lamas and the Karmapas are both lines of this kind, each one recognized as the return of the one before. How is one found? Tradition describes several signs, and searchers weigh them together: a letter the teacher left about where to look, the dreams and visions of senior lamas, omens around a birth, and finally the child, tested with things that were the teacher's. Then a recognition is announced, and the child is raised and educated in the monastery. Tibetan teachers speak about the hard part openly. Recognitions have sometimes been disputed, and politics has sometimes pressed in. And teachers are clear that a title is a beginning, not a finish line: a recognized tulku still has to study for years, take vows, practice, and earn the trust of students like anyone else. What the system holds onto is a thread: a teacher, a monastery, a community of students, and the hope that the one who cared for them has returned.

segments.voice: If something came down to you from an older generation, a ring, a book, a recipe card, hold it in your hands; if not, rest your hands on your knees and think of one thing you know how to do that came down that way. Let the line run backward, who had it before you, and before them, a chain of hands longer than you can see. Then let a quiet thank-you travel down the whole length of it.
Tulku. The emanation body: in Tibet, a teacher recognized as the return of an earlier master, who must still study and practice. Today's word.

1326.title: Tibetan nuns
1326.hook: nunneries rebuilding, and in recent years the first nuns awarded the highest study degree
1326.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist nuns live in nunneries in Tibet, India, Nepal and elsewhere; in some nunneries they follow the full philosophical curriculum, including courtyard debate, and some have been awarded the geshema degree.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tulkus: teachers recognized as the return of earlier masters. Your line: returned.

A row of women with shaved heads and maroon robes stands at the front of a hall. Their teachers are there, and their families, and other nuns who crowded in to watch. One by one, the women step forward to receive a degree, a white scarf, applause. Behind each of them sit years of memorizing, studying and arguing over the same great texts that monks study. The degree has a name: geshema. For a long time it existed only in its other form, geshe, held by monks. Now there are nuns who hold it.
screen: `WOMEN IN MAROON, AT THE FRONT.` → `YEARS OF STUDY BEHIND THEM.` → `THE GESHEMA.`

segments.voice: Tibet has had nuns and nunneries for a long time, often smaller and poorer than the great monasteries, and with less access to the full course of philosophical study. Then came upheaval. Nunneries in Tibet were destroyed or emptied. In exile, in India and Nepal, nuns built again, often from almost nothing: a few rooms, a teacher, a kitchen. Inside Tibet, nunneries were rebuilt too. In exile, some nunneries made a deliberate choice. Their nuns would study the same curriculum as the monks: the Perfection of Wisdom, the Middle Way, logic, the monastic rules. And they would debate it, in their own courtyards, with the same sharp questions. For years it was slow work, finding teachers and building the texts into their days. In recent years, nuns from these programs sat the final examinations, and the geshema degree was awarded: the same top level of study that monks reach with the geshe. Senior lamas publicly supported the step. One question is still open. Tibetan tradition gives nuns the novice ordination, but the lineage of full ordination for women did not take root in Tibet, and how to restore it is still discussed among Tibetan teachers. Some Tibetan nuns have received full ordination in other Buddhist lineages. Different teachers hold different views, and the conversation continues. Meanwhile, in the courtyards, the clapping goes on, and women are doing it.

1327.title: Milarepa's songs
1327.hook: the songs as a practice of their own, sung in caves and kitchens
1327.howItsDone: Kagyu monasteries and retreat centers chant Milarepa's songs, and Tibetan Buddhists sing or recite verses from the Hundred Thousand Songs at gatherings and at home, treating the singing itself as practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tibetan nuns, who rebuilt their nunneries and took up the full course of study. Your line: they study too.

A deer bursts out of the trees, running for its life, and stops at the mouth of a cave. A thin man sits there, worn down by years of living on nettles and little else. He doesn't reach for it. He sings to it. Then a hunting dog comes crashing after, and he sings to the dog. Then the hunter arrives, furious, bow already drawn. The story is told in the songs of Milarepa, the Tibetan hermit-poet. In these stories, when something happened, a visitor, a quarrel, a hard question, a beautiful morning, Milarepa's answer was often a song.
screen: `A DEER AT THE CAVE.` → `A DOG, THEN A HUNTER.` → `THE HERMIT SINGS.`

segments.voice: Tibetans call these songs gur: songs of realization, sung when understanding overflows into words. Milarepa didn't invent the form. Tradition traces it back through his teacher Marpa to the wandering yogis of India, who sang their awakening in short, bright verses. But Milarepa made the form his own. The songs aren't abstract. He sings about the cold, the nettles he ate, his empty cave, his old teacher, the clouds over the mountain. A visitor mocks his poverty, and he sings back about what wealth really holds. A young woman asks why he lives like this, and he sings her an answer. The teaching arrives inside ordinary things. His students remembered the songs and their stories, and later they were gathered into a great collection Tibetans call the Hundred Thousand Songs. They were never meant only to be read. In Kagyu monasteries and retreat centers they are chanted. Some families sing a few verses at home; a cook might hum one while the tea boils. To sing a song of realization is to let the words pass through your own breath and body, and the tradition treats that as practice in its own right, not a performance. A truth you sing goes in differently from a truth you read.

segments.voice: Choose a line you already know and love, a hymn, a mantra from earlier on this path, a lullaby, and sing it softly, out loud, once, noticing the breath it takes and where the sound sits in your chest. Sing it again, a little slower, then listen to the room after the sound ends. If singing feels like too much today, hum it.
Milarepa's songs. The songs of realization of Tibet's hermit-poet, gathered by his students and still sung as practice. Today's word.
Your line: sing it. Nettles, clouds and an empty cave, all set to a tune. Back tomorrow.

1328.title: Thangka painting
1328.hook: painted scrolls made by exact rules, used in meditation
1328.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists hang thangkas in homes, temples and retreat rooms; trained painters make them to set proportions, a lama consecrates them, and practitioners gaze at them to support visualization in meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Milarepa's songs, sung to a deer, a dog and a furious hunter. Your line: sing it.

A painter sits on a cushion with a stretched piece of cotton propped in front of her. She hasn't drawn a single face yet. With a ruler and a fine charcoal line, she is drawing a grid: a center line, cross lines, careful measured marks, like a builder laying out a house. Only when the grid is right does the figure begin: the head here, the heart there, the hands exactly so many units from the center. It will take a long time. The finished painting can be rolled up and carried on a horse. It's a thangka.
screen: `A GRID BEFORE A FACE.` → `HEAD HERE, HEART THERE.` → `ROLLED UP, CARRIED ON A HORSE.`

segments.voice: A thangka is a Tibetan painted scroll, usually on cotton, framed in silk brocade and fitted with a rod so it can be rolled up. It could travel with a teacher or a nomad family and be hung wherever the practice happened that day. Some monasteries keep giant thangkas that are unrolled across a hillside on festival days. Thangka painters learn measurement systems handed down in texts and from master to student. Each kind of figure has its proportions, a peaceful buddha one set, a wrathful protector another, and a painter isn't free to stretch a face or shrink a hand for effect. The rules carry the teaching, so a figure painted today matches the figure described long ago. The colors are traditionally ground from minerals and plants, sometimes with gold, and painters train for years under a teacher. Tradition says the eyes are often painted last; then a lama consecrates the painting, and it is understood to be more than a picture: a support for the presence of what it shows. And a thangka is made to be looked at in meditation. A practitioner gazes at the figure, the hands, the colors, the ornaments, then closes the eyes and builds it again in the mind. Here the exact rules matter most. A face drawn by whim would be a different face each time. A face painted by rule can be held steady, by many people, across generations.
screen: `A SCROLL THAT ROLLS AND TRAVELS.` · `PROPORTIONS HANDED DOWN.` · `MINERAL COLORS, EYES LAST.` · `GAZE, CLOSE THE EYES, REBUILD.` · then, large: `PAINTED BY RULE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on one painting, a thangka found online, a print on your wall, a photo you love, taking in the whole first, then going slowly detail by detail: a hand, a color, a small thing in a corner you never noticed. When you feel you've really seen it, close your eyes and see it again as clearly as you can. Then open them, and look at what you missed.
Thangka. A Tibetan painted scroll, made to exact proportions with mineral colors, and used as a support for meditation. Today's word.

1329.title: The Himalayas
1329.hook: Bhutan, Ladakh, Sikkim, Nepal: Vajrayana in the mountains
1329.howItsDone: Vajrayana Buddhists in Bhutan, Ladakh, Sikkim and Nepal keep their own lineages, monasteries and festivals, and these regions also became homes for Tibetan teachers in exile.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thangka, a scroll painted by rule and rolled up to travel. Your line: painted by rule.

The Tiger's Nest. That's what people call a monastery that clings to a cliff face, white walls and golden roofs, hanging over a drop so steep that clouds drift below it. Pilgrims climb a long, narrow path to reach it. And it isn't in Tibet. It's in Bhutan. Tradition says Padmasambhava, a teacher Tibetan tradition honors as a second Buddha, flew there on the back of a tigress and meditated in a cave in the rock. Tibet gave the Vajrayana much of its shape, but this path has long lived across the whole roof of the world.
screen: `A MONASTERY ON A CLIFF.` → `THE TIGER'S NEST, IN BHUTAN.` → `ACROSS THE ROOF OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Bhutan is a small kingdom east of Nepal where the Vajrayana runs through public life. Its great fortress-monasteries, called dzongs, often hold government offices on one side of the courtyard and monks on the other. The Drukpa Kagyu lineage is at the heart of its religious life, and festivals there fill courtyards with masked dancers. Ladakh is a high, dry land in India's far north, all brown mountains and blue sky. Monasteries such as Thiksey rise on hilltops above the villages, prayer flags snapping in the wind, and Ladakhi Buddhists keep traditions close to Tibet's, in their own language and with their own festivals. Sikkim is a small Indian state on the slopes below Kangchenjunga, with green valleys and monasteries tucked into forest. Rumtek, near its capital, became a seat of the Karma Kagyu lineage after its teachers left Tibet. In Nepal, in Kathmandu, the great white dome of Boudhanath stupa looks out over the city with painted eyes, and Tibetan, Sherpa and Nepali Buddhists walk around it, clockwise, turning prayer wheels. Nepal also holds Lumbini, which Buddhists honor as the place where the Buddha was born. These places didn't simply borrow a religion. Each has its own lineages, saints and ways of practice. And when Tibetan teachers went into exile, some found shelter in these same mountains, among people who already chanted the same mantras.
screen: `BHUTAN: DZONGS AND MASKED DANCES.` · `LADAKH: HILLTOP MONASTERIES.` · `SIKKIM: RUMTEK IN THE FOREST.` · `NEPAL: BOUDHANATH'S PAINTED EYES.` · then, large: `IN THE MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: Open a map, or picture one, find the long curve of the Himalayas, and place them one by one: Ladakh in the west, then Nepal, then Sikkim, then Bhutan, with Tibet to the north. Linger on each name for a breath, and think of a monastery bell ringing there right now, someone turning a prayer wheel, someone climbing toward a cliff. Then set the map down and rest with the breath.

1330.title: Mongolia's Buddhism
1330.hook: Vajrayana among the Mongols, and its return since 1990
1330.howItsDone: In Mongolia, Buddhists visit monasteries such as Gandan in Ulaanbaatar to turn prayer wheels, make offerings and hear chanting, and monasteries have been rebuilt and young monks trained since the end of the communist era.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Himalayas: Bhutan, Ladakh, Sikkim and Nepal. Your line: in the mountains.

An old man in a long padded coat turns a row of prayer wheels, one after another, at a monastery on a hill in Ulaanbaatar, his breath white in the cold. Behind him, a line of boys in maroon robes hurries toward the assembly hall, late for chanting. The old man remembers when the halls were silent and the robes were gone. The boys never knew that. They just know the chanting starts at a certain hour, and they're late. Between his memory and their rush is the story of Mongolia's Buddhism.
screen: `A COLD MORNING IN ULAANBAATAR.` → `AN OLD MAN, A PRAYER WHEEL.` → `BOYS LATE FOR CHANTING.`

segments.voice: Mongol rulers and Tibetan lamas met more than once in history, and one meeting stands out. A Mongol ruler, Altan Khan, met the Gelug teacher Sonam Gyatso and gave him a title, Dalai: the Mongolian word for ocean. Tradition says that is where the name Dalai Lama comes from. Mongolia took up Tibetan Buddhism deeply, with its own monasteries, its own scholars writing in Tibetan, and its own tulkus. One of them, Zanabazar, was a Mongol prince who became a great teacher and also an artist. His gilded bronze buddhas, calm and graceful, are still treasured in Mongolia. He worked within the same rules as the thangka painters and made something unmistakably Mongolian. Then came the silence. Under communist rule, religion was crushed. Monasteries were closed and torn down, monks were killed or forced out of their robes, and practice went underground or disappeared. In the capital, one monastery, Gandan, was allowed to function in a limited way. For a long time, that was nearly all. When the communist era ended, the doors opened. Old monks who had kept their vows in secret came forward to teach. Monasteries were rebuilt, young monks were trained, texts were printed again, and families brought children to the temples. It isn't the same as before; some things were lost for good. But this week keeps finding the same shape: a thing broken, and people who carried it back.
screen: `ALTAN KHAN AND THE OCEAN TITLE.` · `ZANABAZAR'S GILDED BUDDHAS.` · `THE SILENCE: MONASTERIES CLOSED.` · `THE DOORS OPEN AGAIN.` · then, large: `IT RETURNED.`

segments.voice: Think of something that was nearly lost and came back, a language a grandparent spoke, a recipe written down just in time, a friendship mended, and picture the people who did the slow work of bringing it back. Then let this week's others join them, nuns who rebuilt nunneries, teachers who returned, songs still sung, and rest with them.
Mongolia's Buddhism. Tibetan Buddhism made Mongolian, silenced under communist rule, and returning since that era ended. Today's word.
